strengths: The paper introduces a novel and well-motivated notion of group fairness for optimal transport: constraining the group-marginal coupling π_SW of a transport plan to match a target F ∈ Π(p, q). This is modular, accommodates a central planner's preferences (quotas, homogamy limits), and fills a genuine gap between individual fairness in matching (Gale–Shapley line of work) and fairness-via-OT for downstream predictions.

The theory is substantive: Proposition 3.3 gives an exact Sinkhorn-like structure for the constrained problem (extra group-level scaling), Theorem 4.2 establishes a 1/√n sample complexity bound for the fairness-penalized entropic OT problem matching the best known rates for unpenalized entropic OT, and Theorem 4.4 provides a uniform-over-Θ deviation bound for the fairness loss of transport plans computed with learned costs, generalizing Rigollet & Strømme. The proofs in the appendix are reasonably detailed and the proof techniques (linearization of the convex penalty, sandwiching, rescaling of dual potentials) are plausible and, to my knowledge, correct in outline.

The two relaxation strategies (convex penalization solved by generalized conditional gradient, and bilevel cost learning) are complementary, and the paper honestly compares their convexity/interpretability/reusability trade-offs rather than overselling one.
The reusability experiment (Figure 7) demonstrating 3–4 orders of magnitude inference-time savings of learned costs over re-solving the penalized problem is a useful practical contribution.
Related work is well surveyed and the paper clearly positions itself against Nguyen et al. (2025), Lobo et al., and constrained OT literature.
weaknesses: Experiments are exclusively on synthetic data (Gaussian mixtures, concentric circles) with very small sample sizes (n = 20 per subgroup, n₀ = 200). The paper motivates the work with school assignment, dating apps, and kidney exchange, but evaluates on none of these or any real dataset, and no baselines from the fair-matching literature (e.g., Lobo et al.) are compared. The empirical significance of the claims is therefore limited.

The convergence claim for FairSinkhorn (Remark 1) is asserted by analogy with alternating projections [4], but the fairness update is a group-level KL-type rescaling, not an orthogonal Euclidean projection; the cited result does not straightforwardly apply, and no convergence rate or proof of the claim for the full algorithm is provided.

Assumption mismatches between statements and proofs: Theorem 4.2 states Assumptions 3.1 and 4.1 (compact support, C^∞ cost), but the proof additionally assumes the cost is L-Lipschitz continuous; this should be in the theorem statement.

Presentation is sloppy in places, undermining confidence: Sections 5.1 and 5.2 are duplicated ('Approaches and Metrics' twice with slightly different text), the appendix contains unresolved citation placeholders ('as proposed in ? ]', 'we found Adam [ ? ]'), the caption of Figure 5 describes circular data as '2D Gaussians', and the Figure 5 legend shows labels (w=0, w=1) inconsistent with the stated three groups.

No error bars or statistical variability are reported; conclusions from plots with ~10-40 points per configuration are hard to assess. The utility metric is restricted to KL divergence to the unconstrained plan and total cost difference; matched-pair quality (e.g., distances of matched individuals), which matters most in matching applications, is not analyzed.

The fairness targets tested are essentially a single family (anti-diagonal targets); the flexibility advertised in the framework is not exercised empirically. The price of fairness is shown only qualitatively.

Reproducibility is uncertain: code 'will be made public upon publication' and is not included; combined with missing hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, independent verification is difficult at review time. There is also no dedicated limitations or research-ethics discussion, which is notable for a paper about enforcing demographic properties in matching systems.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely under-explored problem: enforcing group-level matching quotas directly on optimal transport plans, which the related-work section convincingly argues has not been previously considered (existing fair-OT work uses OT as an auxiliary tool for downstream prediction).

The formal framework is clean: fairness targets F are defined as couplings between group marginals p and q, and the finite-sample problem (3) retains a Sinkhorn-like structure (Proposition 3.3 / Algorithm 1), yielding a practical algorithm (FairSinkhorn).

Two complementary relaxation strategies are developed with appropriate trade-off discussion (convexity vs. reusability in Section 4.3), and the penalized formulation is claimed to generalize to arbitrary convex penalties.

Theoretical contributions are reasonable: Theorem 4.2 shows the fairness penalty does not degrade the 1/sqrt(n) sample complexity of entropic OT, and Theorem 4.4 provides a uniform-over-theta deviation bound for fairness of plans computed on unseen samples with learned costs. The proof techniques (sandwiching, linearization via generalized conditional gradient optimality conditions, extension of Rigollet–Stromme to parametrized bounded costs) are coherent and mostly self-contained in the appendix.
The reusability experiment (Figure 7) demonstrates a practical advantage of cost learning (3–4 orders of magnitude lower inference time), which is a concrete, useful observation.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is very weak for an ICML main-track paper. All experiments are on tiny synthetic datasets (20 samples per subgroup in Figures 3 and 5; n0 = 200 in Figure 7) despite the paper's motivating applications (school assignment, dating apps, kidney exchange). No real-world dataset is used anywhere, so the central claim that the trade-offs matter 'in practice' is not substantiated.

There are no external baselines: the comparison is only among the authors' own methods (FairSinkhorn, penalized OT, cost learning). Competing constrained-OT formulations (e.g., solving (3) as a linearly constrained problem with an LP or other constrained OT solvers) are never benchmarked, so it is unclear whether the proposed solvers are actually the right tools for the problem.

The manuscript is notably sloppy, which undermines confidence in care of execution: Sections 5.1 and 5.2 are duplicated verbatim ('Approaches and Metrics' appears twice); the text cites 'Theorem 4.1' and 'Theorem 4.2' for cost parameterizations that are actually Examples 4.1 and 4.2; Figure 5's caption describes circular data as '2D gaussians'; broken citations appear as '[? ]' in Appendix C (Adam and Sinkhorn-Knopp references); the appendix heading 'B.1 Proof of Theorem 3.2' refers to Proposition 3.2; Theorem 4.2 states O(1/sqrt(n^{-1})); and multiple grammatical errors ('This demonstrate', 'One of the peaks of our cost learning', 'de Mahalanobis').

The convergence guarantee for FairSinkhorn is asserted only via a one-line Remark 1 appealing to [4] for alternating projections on linear constraint sets, with no rate, no discussion of when the fairness projection step yields contraction, and no numerical convergence study. For the paper's core algorithm this is insufficient.

Theorem 4.4's proof explicitly assumes 'for simplicity' that the fairness penalty is independent of the cost function, which weakens the theoretical support for the cost-learning pipeline actually used in the experiments; moreover, the bound's exp(5*R_Theta/epsilon) dependence is acknowledged as worst-case unavoidable but its practical tightness is never explored.

The fairness notion itself has a significant conceptual limitation that is never discussed: enforcing group-level mass quotas (pi_SW = F) says nothing about within-group treatment; a plan can satisfy the target exactly while being highly individual-unfair within a group. For a paper whose motivation is normative fairness, this limitation, the political/legal sensitivity of imposing matching quotas, and potential harms are not discussed at all — the paper has no limitations section and no ethics/broader-impact discussion, which is a notable omission for a fairness-focused contribution.

The utility metrics are defined only relative to the non-fair OT plan (KL divergence between plans, cost difference), which makes 'Pareto front' language somewhat circular and hinders comparison to any absolute notion of matching quality or welfare.

Reproducibility is limited: code is only promised 'upon publication', and given the small synthetic setups and the implementation irregularities in Appendix C, independent verification would be difficult.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely novel and underexplored problem: enforcing explicit group-level mass constraints (matching quotas) directly on optimal transport plans, which the authors convincingly differentiate from prior work on fairness in matching (GS-type mechanisms, kidney exchange) and fairness-via-OT for prediction tasks.

The FairSinkhorn algorithm is a natural and elegant extension of Sinkhorn to exact fairness constraints, with a clean structural result (Proposition 3.3) showing the fair plan has a Sinkhorn-like form diag(e^{f/eps})(K ⊙ H)diag(e^{g/eps}), derived from first-order conditions on the Lagrangian.

Theorem 4.2 (sample complexity of fairness-penalized entropic OT) is a nice result of independent interest: the proof technique of sandwiching the penalized objective between linearized entropic OT problems (Appendix B.2) is clean and extends to generic convex penalties.

Theorem 4.4 provides a uniform-over-parameters deviation bound for the fairness loss with learned costs, generalizing Rigollet & Stromme to parameterized cost families—this directly supports the practical reusability claim of the cost-learning approach.

The paper is well organized in terms of problem motivation: the relaxed constraint formulation (Section 4) is properly motivated by the price-of-fairness phenomenon, and Section 4.3 honestly compares convexity, flexibility, and reusability trade-offs of the two approaches.

Experiments include a dedicated reusability study (Figure 7) demonstrating 3-4 orders of magnitude inference-time savings for learned costs, which directly validates the claimed practical advantage over penalized OT.
weaknesses: All experiments are on purely synthetic data (Gaussian mixtures and concentric circles) with very small sample sizes (n_x = n_y = 20 per subgroup). The motivating applications (dating apps, school assignment, kidney exchange) are never evaluated empirically, so the practical relevance of the fairness notion and the claimed trade-offs remain unverified on real matching problems.

There are no external baselines: the comparisons are entirely among the authors' own methods (FairSinkhorn, penalized OT, cost learning). Obvious alternatives—e.g., solving the fair problem as a linear program, group-wise transport with adjusted marginals, or a simple cost-augmentation scheme—are absent, making it hard to assess whether the proposed machinery is needed.

The convergence guarantee for FairSinkhorn is only asserted in Remark 1 ('alternates between projections on sets defined by linear constraints, it is guaranteed to converge [4]'), but the update L ← F ⊘ Φ(u, v) is a multiplicative scaling, not a Euclidean projection onto a convex set; the argument is incomplete and no convergence rate is given.

The main theoretical results are close extensions of existing machinery: Theorem 4.2 attains the same O(1/√n) rate as Genevay et al. and Mena & Niles-Weed via linearization, and Theorem 4.4 rescales Rigollet & Stromme's proof; the exp(5RΘ ε^{-1}) dependence makes the bound practically vacuous for small ε, and the paper does not quantify how restrictive this is beyond citing worst-case necessity.

The manuscript contains notable presentation defects: Sections 5.1 and 5.2 are duplicated ('Approaches and Metrics' appears twice with near-identical text); broken citations ('? ]') in the appendix (Adam reference and Sinkhorn-Knopp reference); inconsistent cross-references in Section 5.1 (Experiments cite 'Theorem 4.1' and 'Theorem 4.2' for cost parameterizations that are Examples 4.1/4.2); notation errors such as 'O(1/√n^{-1})' in Theorem 4.2 as stated in Appendix B.2; typos ('de Mahalanobis', 'One of the peaks'); and the fairness target used in all experiments ('all coefficients zero except anti-diagonal entries 1/(K_s K_w)') does not appear to be a valid coupling of p and q as required by the framework, which is confusing.

There is no limitations or ethics discussion despite the paper being explicitly about fairness in socially consequential allocation mechanisms; notably, enforcing matching quotas deterministically on individuals raises legitimate ethical questions (e.g., overriding individual preferences) that deserve at least acknowledgment.

Reproducibility is limited: code is only promised upon publication, several experimental details rely on package defaults, and the small-scale synthetic setups (plus the unexplained fairness target) make independent replication of the reported trade-off curves difficult.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: imposing explicit group-wise mass constraints (fairness targets) on the OT plan itself, which the authors convincingly argue has not been previously considered (prior fairness-OT work uses OT as a tool for downstream prediction). The framework flexibly covers homogamy limits, quotas (four-fifths rule, EU directive), etc.

Clean technical treatment of the exact-fairness problem: the dual characterization (Prop. 3.3) showing the fair plan has Sinkhorn-like form with an extra group-level potential H leads naturally to the FairSinkhorn algorithm, which is a minimal and elegant modification of Sinkhorn-Knopp.

Meaningful theoretical results: a finite-sample O(1/√n) bound for penalized entropic OT matching the rate of standard entropic OT (showing the fairness penalty does not degrade statistical efficiency), and a uniform-over-parameter-family deviation bound for fairness of plans computed with a learned cost on unseen samples, giving a fairness generalization guarantee for the reusability property.

Well-differentiated related work: the paper carefully positions itself against fairness in matching mechanisms (Gale-Shapley variants, kidney exchange), fair bipartite graph matching, fairness-via-OT literature, and constrained/statistical OT, including an extended appendix review.

Exercises include a fairness-cost trade-off analysis, an inference-time/reusability experiment for learned costs, and a deterministic-sampling check (Fig. 7b); code is released and implementation details (solvers, grids, hyperparameters) are given in Appendix D.

Thoughtful impact statement acknowledging that the choice of fairness target is a political/ethical decision rather than something the method prescribes; honest limitations discussion (group fairness only, open fairness-bias trade-off question, downstream outcomes unmodeled).
weaknesses: No convergence analysis for FairSinkhorn: Proposition 3.3 characterizes the optimum but the algorithm's convergence to that optimum (existence/uniqueness of the fixed point of the modified Sinkhorn iteration) is only assessed empirically (Fig. 7a, 'qualitatively similar rates'). This is a significant gap for the paper's headline algorithm.

Theoretical contributions, while correct-looking, are largely extensions of existing machinery (Genevay et al. 2019, Mena & Niles-Weed 2019, Rigollet & Stromme 2025, Rakotomamonjy et al. 2015); the bounds inherit exponential dependence on ε^{-1} and λ (e.g., scaling breaks down when λKsKw ≳ ‖c‖∞/ε), limiting their practical guidance, and constants are hidden behind ≲.

Experimental scale and baselines are limited: synthetic experiments use only 250/25 samples, and the semi-synthetic experiment is a subsampled Kaggle dating dataset with hand-constructed compatibility and cost functions. There is no comparison against alternative approaches for the constrained OT problem (e.g., a general-purpose constrained LP/QP solver, or existing constrained/structured OT methods), so it is hard to assess whether the proposed machinery is practically superior to naive alternatives.

The cost-learning approach is non-convex bilevel optimization with only empirical evidence of success; no analysis of local minima, initialization sensitivity, or when the parametric family can even represent a fair plan (the Mahalanobis family demonstrably cannot reach fairness below 10^-2 on the Circles data).

The relaxation from exact constraints to the penalized objective uses a squared penalty whose solution need not satisfy any prescribed tolerance ρ; the connection between the penalty parameter λ and the actual fairness violation level is only explored empirically, not theoretically.

Presentation issues: several typos and minor errors ('O(1/√n −1)' in Theorem 4.2's formal statement, 'The the cost learning approach', 'a throughout analysis', 'assignements', 'symmetrical arguments', notation switching between Πϵ and Πε), which while not fatal, suggest insufficient proofreading.

The empirical fairness measurement in experiments is with respect to sample-level empirical group frequencies; no experiment probes sensitivity to the assumed fairness target F or to estimation error in group probabilities p, q when they must be estimated from data.

strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely novel and well-motivated problem setting: enforcing explicit group-pair mass constraints ('fairness targets') directly on optimal transport plans between two populations with sensitive attributes. The authors make a convincing case that this setting is distinct from prior work on fair matching (Gale-Shapley-style, KPD, bipartite graph matching) and from prior OT-fairness work where OT is merely a tool for downstream prediction (Section 2, Appendix A).

The technical development is coherent and reasonably self-contained: the dual characterization (Prop 3.3 / B.1) leading to the FairSinkhorn algorithm is clean, the existence/uniqueness result (Prop 3.2) is properly proven, and the two relaxation strategies (convex penalized OT and bilevel cost learning) are well differentiated, including an honest discussion of their relative trade-offs (convexity, flexibility, reusability, interpretability, Section 4.3).

The two theoretical results are meaningful: (i) an O(n^{-1/2}) sample complexity bound for the penalized entropic OT objective (Theorem 4.2), shown not to degrade statistical efficiency relative to standard entropic OT; and (ii) a uniform-over-theta deviation bound on the fairness of plans computed on unseen data with a learned cost (Theorem 4.4), which directly supports the 'reusable cost' claim. The proofs in Appendices C.2-C.3 build carefully on Genevay et al. (2019), Rakotomamonjy et al. (2015), and Rigollet & Stromme (2025).

Experiments cover the important aspects: exact vs. penalized fairness trade-off (Fig 3a), penalized vs. cost learning across different data geometries (Fig 3b), reusability/generalization of learned costs with inference time (Fig 4), deterministic sampling from fair plans (Fig 7b), convergence speed of FairSinkhorn (Fig 7a), and a multi-group, high-dimensional semi-synthetic dating experiment (Fig 5). Code is publicly released and implementation details are thorough.

The paper treats ethics and limitations seriously: an explicit impact statement stresses that the fairness target is a political/ethical choice not prescribed by the method, and the limitations section honestly identifies the restriction to group fairness, the open fairness-bias trade-off analysis, and unmodeled downstream effects.
weaknesses: The theoretical contributions, while correct and useful, are extensions of existing machinery rather than fundamentally new analysis: Theorem 4.2 and Theorem 4.4 both reduce to sample complexity results of Genevay et al. (2019) and Rigollet & Stromme (2025) via linearization/rescaling. The constants inherit an exponential dependence on epsilon (and on lambda, quantified only in Appendix C.2), which is acknowledged but weakens practical relevance of the bounds.

Theorem 4.2 as stated omits the dependency on epsilon and lambda from the main text ('we provide more details in Section C.2'), and the theorem statement in Appendix C.2 introduces an additional L-Lipschitz assumption not mentioned in the main-text version; the displayed bound O(1/sqrt{n^{-1}}) also contains a typo. These presentation issues undermine confidence in careful checking.

There is no convergence guarantee for FairSinkhorn itself; only empirical convergence qualitatively similar to Sinkhorn is shown (Fig 7a). Given that the algorithm alternates projections onto linear constraint sets, a theoretical convergence statement (or at least a discussion of when the scheme can stall, e.g., feasibility issues) would be expected.

The empirical evaluation is modest in scale and scope: synthetic experiments use only 250/25 samples with two groups, and the semi-synthetic dating experiment relies on a Kaggle dataset with manually constructed compatibility and subsampling to US demographics. There are no comparisons to alternative constrained-OT baselines (e.g., general constrained OT solvers, mass-constrained OT of Korman & McCann, or feasible-side methods) that could contextualize the cost-fairness frontier.

The fairness notion, while flexibly presented, amounts to imposing linear marginal constraints on the coupling over a partition of the two populations. The paper does not analyze the 'price of fairness' theoretically (acknowledged as open), nor what targets are practically attainable at acceptable cost, which limits actionable guidance for the central-planner use case motivating the work.

Minor but noticeable inconsistencies and typos reduce polish: Example 4.1/4.2 in the text are referred to as 'Theorem 4.1'/'Theorem 4.2'; 'Fsv' vs 'Fsw' in Section 4.2; the test-set sizes for Figure 4 are described as 500/50 in the main text but 500/500 in Appendix D.2; Proposition 3.2 is proved as 'Theorem 3.2' in the appendix; Lemma C.1 is labeled 'Lennma'.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: imposing group-level mass constraints (fairness targets) directly on the OT plan is, as far as the related work shows, previously unexplored, and the paper carefully distinguishes its setting from fairness in GS-type mechanisms, bipartite graph matching, and OT-as-tool-for-fair-prediction (Nguyen et al. 2025).

The FairSinkhorn algorithm is an elegant and natural extension of Sinkhorn: the Lagrangian analysis (Proposition 3.3 / B.1) cleanly shows that the fairness multipliers enter as a block-constant additive structure in the kernel, making implementation simple and reusable; the derivation in Appendix B is correct and easy to verify.

Two genuinely useful theoretical results: Theorem 4.2 gives an O(n^{-1/2}) sample complexity bound for fairness-penalized entropic OT via a sandwich argument (lower bound through linearization à la Rakotomamonjy et al., upper bound through optimality conditions), and Theorem 4.4 gives a uniform-over-parameter-family deviation bound for the fairness of cost-learned plans on unseen data, generalizing Rigollet & Stromme (2025). The proofs are sketched convincingly and detailed in the appendix.

The comparison between the penalized and cost-learning approaches (Section 4.3) is honest and insightful: convexity vs. bilevel non-convexity, flexibility vs. reusability, and the experiments empirically confirm these trade-offs (e.g., penalized OT dominates on the Circles dataset; the Mahalanobis parameterization cannot reach the target there while the MLP can).

Good treatment of limitations and ethics: the impact statement explicitly notes that choosing the fairness target is a political/ethical decision outside the scope of the method, the limitations section is candid about the restriction to group fairness, and code is released, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: No convergence guarantee for FairSinkhorn, the headline algorithm. Proposition 3.3 only characterizes the fixed-point form of the solution; the appendix proves the structural form but never establishes that the alternating iteration in Algorithm 1 converges to it. The claim of 'qualitatively similar rates' rests solely on one empirical plot (Figure 7a) on a single synthetic configuration. This is a notable soundness gap for a paper whose first contribution is the algorithm.

The empirical evaluation is small-scale and thin on baselines. Key synthetic experiments use only 250 samples from X and 25 from Y; the semi-synthetic dating experiment uses a Kaggle dataset with hand-constructed compatibility matrices and an independence target F = p q^T, which is arguably the least informative possible target. There is no real-world experiment and no comparison against any alternative constrained-OT or post-processing baseline beyond vanilla entropic OT with varying ε, which is a weak baseline.

The theoretical constants may limit practical relevance: the sample complexity bound inherits an exponential dependence on ||c||_∞/ε and on λ (e^{λKsKw/ε}), as the authors themselves discuss (Appendix C.2); similarly Theorem 4.4 carries exp(5R_Θ/ε). No experiments probe whether these bounds are informative at practical parameter values, so the 'fairness guarantees on unseen data' claim is qualitative at best.

Theorem 4.2 bounds the deviation of the penalized objective value only, not the fairness violation or the plan itself, so the statistical guarantee does not directly control the quantity practitioners care about (fairness of the estimated plan); the fairness-relevant guarantee only covers the cost-learning route.

Some sloppiness in presentation: the experiments section cites 'Mahalanobis cost (Theorem 4.1) and neural cost (Theorem 4.2)' when these are Examples 4.1/4.2; minor typos ('The the cost learning approach', 'a throughout analysis'); Lemma C.1's construction divides by p(s)q(w) without addressing degenerate groups. These do not undermine the core but indicate the manuscript could be tighter.

The fairness notion itself involves value-laden design choices (matching quotas can conflict with individual preferences or have adverse distributive effects); the paper acknowledges this in the impact statement, but there is no analysis of what the fairness-cost trade-off implies for the individuals being matched (e.g., utility loss distribution across groups), which the limitations section defers to future work.
